question: How does the AI Act define the risk management system for a high-risk AI system, and is it a one-time or ongoing process?
gold: It is a continuous, iterative process planned and run throughout the entire lifecycle of the high-risk AI system, requiring regular systematic review and updating (Art. 9(2)). It must be established, implemented, documented and maintained (Art. 9(1)).
grading_rule: Must state continuous/iterative/lifecycle, not one-time. Bonus for naming the four steps in 9(2)(a)-(d).

question: For high-risk AI systems listed in points 2 to 8 of Annex III, which conformity assessment procedure must the provider follow, and does it require a notified body?
gold: The internal control procedure referred to in Annex VI, which does not provide for the involvement of a notified body (Art. 43(2)).
grading_rule: Must say internal control / Annex VI AND 'no notified body'. Omitting the no-notified-body part is partial.

question: Under the GDPR, is processing biometric data for the purpose of uniquely identifying a person permitted, and what is the default rule?
gold: By default it is prohibited. Art. 9(1) prohibits processing of special categories of personal data, which includes biometric data processed for the purpose of uniquely identifying a natural person. The prohibition lifts only if a GDPR Art. 9(2) exception applies (e.g. explicit consent, substantial public interest).
grading_rule: Must state the prohibition AND acknowledge the 9(2) exceptions exist. 'Prohibited, full stop' with no mention of exceptions is partial - it is legally misleading.

question: When a product contains an AI system that falls under both the AI Act and Union harmonisation legislation listed in Section A of Annex I, who is responsible for ensuring the product complies with all applicable requirements?
gold: The provider. Art. 8(2) makes providers responsible for ensuring their product is fully compliant with all applicable requirements under the applicable Union harmonisation legislation.
grading_rule: Must identify the provider. Bonus for noting the provider may integrate AI Act testing/documentation into existing Annex I procedures.

question: What must a provider have established to demonstrate that a high-risk AI system complies with the requirements of Section 2, and who does that obligation fall on?
gold: A provider must establish a risk management system. Art. 8(1) requires the risk management system referred to in Article 9 to be taken into account when ensuring compliance. Art. 9 defines it as a continuous, iterative lifecycle process comprising risk identification/analysis, risk estimation under intended use and reasonably foreseeable misuse, evaluation of post-market-monitoring risks, and adoption of targeted risk management measures (Art. 9(2)(a)-(d)). The obligation falls on the provider (Art. 9(9)).
grading_rule: Must (a) name the risk management system and (b) attribute it to the provider. Must have followed the Art. 8 -> Art. 9 reference, not answered from Art. 8 alone. Bonus for the lifecycle/iterative characterisation.
canary: If REFERENCES (Art.8->Art.9), IMPOSES (Art.9->RMS), or APPLIES_TO (->provider) is missing from the graph, this question fails.

question: Before a high-risk AI system is placed on the market, what testing must be done and against what criteria?
gold: High-risk AI systems must be tested to identify the most appropriate risk management measures and to ensure consistent performance and compliance with Section 2 (Art. 9(6)). Testing must occur at any time throughout development and, in any event, prior to placing on the market or putting into service (Art. 9(8)), carried out against prior-defined metrics and probabilistic thresholds appropriate to the intended purpose (Art. 9(8)). Testing may include real-world conditions in accordance with Article 60 (Art. 9(7)).
grading_rule: Must state timing (before market placement) AND 'prior-defined metrics / probabilistic thresholds'. Bonus for the Art. 60 real-world-testing reference.

question: A provider of a high-risk AI system intended for use by law enforcement wants to use the Annex VII conformity assessment, but no harmonised standards exist for it. Who must act as the notified body, and where is that authority defined?
gold: Because no harmonised standards exist, the provider must follow the Annex VII procedure (Art. 43(1)). Normally the provider may choose any notified body, but where the system is intended for law enforcement, immigration, or asylum authorities (or Union institutions), the market surveillance authority referred to in Article 74(8) or (9) shall act as the notified body (Art. 43(1)). For Annex III point 1 systems used for law enforcement, Art. 74(8) designates that authority as the competent data protection supervisory authority (under GDPR or Directive (EU) 2016/680), or another authority designated under Arts. 41-44 of Directive (EU) 2016/680. The term 'market surveillance authority' is itself defined in Art. 3(26) as the national authority acting under Regulation (EU) 2019/1020.
grading_rule: correct requires the chain: no standards -> Annex VII -> law-enforcement carve-out -> data protection supervisory authority acts as notified body. Naming Art. 74(8) as the designation source is required; Art. 3(26) definition is a bonus. Hardest AIA-only item - expect the vector baseline to fail it.
note: Also touches GDPR via the data protection authority, but kept as a pure AIA three-hop. The clean cross-regulation item is xr-001.

question: The AI Act refers to 'special categories of personal data'. Where does that term come from, and what does it mean for an emotion recognition system that processes biometric data?
gold: The AI Act does not define the term itself - Art. 3(37) AIA defines it by reference to Article 9(1) of the GDPR (Regulation (EU) 2016/679), plus Art. 10 of Directive (EU) 2016/680 and Art. 10(1) of Regulation (EU) 2018/1725. Under GDPR Art. 9(1), biometric data processed to uniquely identify a person is a special category, and processing is prohibited unless a GDPR Art. 9(2) exception applies. An 'emotion recognition system' is defined in AIA Art. 3(39) as a system inferring emotions from a person's biometric data. Where that biometric data is used to uniquely identify individuals, the GDPR Art. 9 prohibition and exception regime govern the lawfulness of processing, independently of the AI Act's own obligations.
grading_rule: RETRIEVAL-focused. correct = retrieved Art. 3(37), GDPR Art. 9, and Art. 3(39), and faithfully stated the cross-reference + the prohibition. The final legal-synthesis sentence is reasoning, not a quote - treat as bonus, do not require for a pass. The hop is explicit in the text, so a failure here is a traversal failure, not a guessing failure.

question: List the main obligations the AI Act places on deployers of high-risk AI systems.
gold: Under Article 26, deployers of high-risk AI systems must: (1) take appropriate technical and organisational measures to use the system in accordance with its instructions for use (Art. 26(1)); (2) assign human oversight to natural persons with the necessary competence, training, authority and support (Art. 26(2)); (3) where they control the input data, ensure input data is relevant and sufficiently representative for the intended purpose (Art. 26(4)); (4) monitor the system's operation, inform the provider/distributor and market surveillance authority and suspend use where it may present a risk under Art. 79(1), and report serious incidents (Art. 26(5)); (5) keep the automatically generated logs under their control for at least six months unless other law provides otherwise (Art. 26(6)); (6) where the deployer is an employer, inform workers' representatives and affected workers before workplace use (Art. 26(7)); (7) where the deployer is a public authority or Union body, comply with the registration obligations in Art. 49 and not use an unregistered system (Art. 26(8)); (8) use the provider's Art. 13 information to carry out a data protection impact assessment under GDPR Art. 35 / Directive (EU) 2016/680 Art. 27 where applicable (Art. 26(9)); (9) for post-remote biometric identification in law enforcement, obtain prior (or <=48h) judicial/administrative authorisation with strict limits and documentation (Art. 26(10)); (10) inform natural persons subject to Annex III systems that make or assist decisions about them (Art. 26(11)); (11) cooperate with competent authorities (Art. 26(12)).
grading_rule: correct = names the majority of the eleven Art. 26 obligations with NO invented ones. Art. 27 (FRIA) is a SEPARATE article and is NOT an Art. 26 obligation - listing it is an automatic wrong. Art. 26(9) is a DPIA (GDPR Art. 35), a different instrument. Report recall (how many of the eleven found) and precision (how many listed were real) separately.

question: What is the maximum fine under the AI Act for deploying a prohibited AI system?
gold: Up to EUR 35 000 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 7 % of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher (AIA Art. 99(3)). This is the AI Act's highest penalty tier and it attaches to non-compliance with the prohibition of the AI practices referred to in Article 5. [For SMEs and start-ups, AIA Art. 99(6) inverts the rule to whichever of the amount or percentage is LOWER.]

Retained as a hallucination probe: any figure not supported by the retrieved chunk is wrong. Giving the 15M/3 % deployer tier (Art. 99(4)) or the 7.5M/1 % information tier is wrong. Omitting 'whichever is higher' is partial.

question: A deployer of a high-risk AI system has to carry out a data protection impact assessment. Which regulation imposes that assessment, what does the AI Act tell the deployer to use when producing it, and what must the assessment contain as a minimum?
gold: The AI Act does not itself impose the assessment; it routes to it. Under AIA Art. 26(9), where applicable, deployers of high-risk AI systems shall use the information provided under Article 13 of the AI Act to comply with their obligation to carry out a data protection impact assessment under Article 35 of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR) or Article 27 of Directive (EU) 2016/680. The obligation itself is therefore imposed by GDPR Art. 35 (or the Directive, where that applies instead). As to minimum content, GDPR Art. 35(7) requires the assessment to contain at least: (a) a systematic description of the envisaged processing operations and the purposes of the processing, including where applicable the legitimate interest pursued by the controller; (b) an assessment of the necessity and proportionality of the processing operations in relation to the purposes; (c) an assessment of the risks to the rights and freedoms of data subjects; and (d) the measures envisaged to address those risks, including safeguards, security measures and mechanisms to ensure the protection of personal data and to demonstrate compliance with the GDPR. [The content of the Article 13 information the deployer must use is defined in AIA Art. 13, which is outside the pasted text; the Directive (EU) 2016/680 branch is likewise outside the corpus.]
grading_rule: correct requires BOTH ends of the bridge: (a) naming GDPR Art. 35 as the source of the DPIA obligation, cited to a retrieved aia-art26-para9, AND (b) at least the substance of the four Art. 35(7) contents, cited to a retrieved gdpr-art35-para7. Stating the four contents without the Art. 26(9) routing (or vice versa) is partial. Dropping the 'where applicable' qualifier or asserting the DPIA as unconditional is partial. Attributing the content requirements to the AI Act, or the routing to GDPR, is wrong. A citation to a paragraph not actually retrieved is wrong regardless of accuracy.

question: Which of a deployer's obligations under Article 26 are modified when the deployer is a financial institution, and how?
gold: Two of the deployer's obligations in Article 26 carry a specific carve-out for financial institutions subject to internal governance requirements under Union financial services law. First, the monitoring obligation: under AIA Art. 26(5), second subparagraph, for deployers that are financial institutions subject to requirements regarding their internal governance, arrangements or processes under Union financial services law, the monitoring obligation set out in the first subparagraph is deemed to be fulfilled by complying with the rules on internal governance arrangements, processes and mechanisms pursuant to the relevant financial service law. Second, the log-keeping obligation: under AIA Art. 26(6), second subparagraph, such financial-institution deployers shall maintain the logs as part of the documentation kept pursuant to the relevant Union financial service law (rather than as a standalone obligation). Both are compliance-routing carve-outs: the obligation is satisfied through the existing financial-services regime rather than removed outright.
grading_rule: correct requires BOTH carve-outs — the monitoring deemed-fulfilled rule from a retrieved aia-art26-para5 AND the log-maintenance-as-documentation rule from a retrieved aia-art26-para6. Returning only one is partial. Characterising either as an outright exemption from the obligation (rather than fulfilment via the financial-services regime) is partial. Inventing a carve-out not in the text (e.g. from 26(7) or 26(8)) is wrong. Correct facts cited to a non-retrieved paragraph are wrong.

The six-month floor in AIA Art. 26(6) governs a different object — the logs automatically generated by the high-risk AI system — and does not apply to these reports. question: An AI system listed in Annex III performs a narrow procedural task. Is it high-risk, and what must its provider do?
gold: Not automatically high-risk, but only if a further condition is met, and an obligation attaches either way. Under AIA Art. 6(2), AI systems referred to in Annex III are considered high-risk. However, Art. 6(3) first subparagraph derogates: an Annex III system shall NOT be considered high-risk where it does not pose a significant risk of harm to the health, safety or fundamental rights of natural persons, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision making. That derogation applies where any of the conditions in the second subparagraph is fulfilled, and Art. 6(3)(a) names one of them: the AI system is intended to perform a narrow procedural task. So a genuine narrow-procedural-task system that poses no significant risk is not high-risk. The consequence is set by Art. 6(4): a provider who considers that an Annex III system is not high-risk shall document its assessment before the system is placed on the market or put into service, shall be subject to the registration obligation set out in Article 49(2), and shall, upon request of national competent authorities, provide the documentation of the assessment. [Note: the derogation is conditional on the no-significant-risk test in 6(3); the narrow-task condition alone does not exempt a system that still poses significant risk. The content of the Article 49(2) registration obligation is outside the pasted text.]
grading_rule: correct requires all three links: (1) Annex III => high-risk under a retrieved aia-art6-para2; (2) the 6(3) derogation, keyed to the narrow-procedural-task condition AND its dependence on the no-significant-risk test, under a retrieved aia-art6-para3; (3) the provider's documentation/registration/on-request obligation under a retrieved aia-art6-para4. Missing link 3 (stating not-high-risk but omitting the Art. 6(4) obligation) is partial. Stating the system is exempt without the no-significant-risk qualifier is partial. Calling it flatly high-risk (ignoring 6(3)) is wrong. Any citation to a non-retrieved paragraph is wrong.

question: Is a remote biometric identification system high-risk under the AI Act, and does the same classification apply to a system whose only purpose is confirming a person is who they claim to be?
gold: The two are treated differently. Under AIA Art. 6(2), AI systems referred to in Annex III are high-risk, and Annex III point 1(a) lists remote biometric identification systems within the biometrics area (in so far as their use is permitted under relevant Union or national law). So a remote biometric identification system is high-risk. However, point 1(a) expressly excludes AI systems intended to be used for biometric verification the sole purpose of which is to confirm that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be. A pure verification (one-to-one confirmation) system therefore does not fall under this high-risk listing.
grading_rule: correct requires BOTH halves: remote biometric identification is high-risk (via a retrieved aia-art6-para2 + Annex III point 1(a)), AND pure biometric verification is excluded by the same point. Stating only that biometric ID is high-risk, without the verification carve-out, is partial. Claiming verification is ALSO high-risk is wrong (it ignores the explicit exclusion). Correct facts cited to a non-retrieved chunk are wrong.

question: Under Annex III, which AI systems in the area of employment and workers' management are classified as high-risk?
gold: Under Annex III point 4 (Employment, workers' management and access to self-employment), two categories are high-risk: (a) AI systems intended to be used for the recruitment or selection of natural persons, in particular to place targeted job advertisements, to analyse and filter job applications, and to evaluate candidates; and (b) AI systems intended to be used to make decisions affecting terms of work-related relationships, the promotion or termination of work-related contractual relationships, to allocate tasks based on individual behaviour or personal traits or characteristics, or to monitor and evaluate the performance and behaviour of persons in such relationships.
grading_rule: correct requires both sub-points of Annex III point 4 — recruitment/selection (4(a)) AND work-terms/promotion/termination/task-allocation/performance-monitoring (4(b)) — cited to a retrieved aia-annex3-point4. Returning only one sub-point is partial. Importing use cases from a different Annex III area (e.g. education, essential services) is wrong. Correct content cited to a non-retrieved chunk is wrong.

question: What is the maximum administrative fine for the most serious category of infringement under the AI Act, and how does that compare to the highest fine tier under the GDPR?
gold: The AI Act's top fine ceiling is higher than the GDPR's. Under AIA Art. 99(3), non-compliance with the prohibition of the AI practices referred to in Article 5 is subject to administrative fines of up to EUR 35 000 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 7 % of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher. Under the GDPR, the highest tier is set by Art. 83(5) (and Art. 83(6) for non-compliance with a supervisory-authority order): up to EUR 20 000 000 or, in the case of an undertaking, up to 4 % of total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding financial year, whichever is higher. So the AI Act's maximum (EUR 35 000 000 / 7 %) exceeds the GDPR's maximum (EUR 20 000 000 / 4 %). [The substance of the Article 5 prohibited practices is outside the pasted text; only the penalty figures are asserted here.]
grading_rule: correct requires BOTH ceilings with correct figures pinned to the correct regulation: AIA EUR 35 000 000 / 7 % from a retrieved aia-art99-para3, AND GDPR EUR 20 000 000 / 4 % from a retrieved gdpr-art83-para5, plus the comparison (AIA higher). Transposing the figures between regulations is wrong. Giving one ceiling only is partial. Omitting the 'whichever is higher' basis is partial. Any figure cited to a non-retrieved chunk is wrong.

question: When an authority decides whether to impose a fine and how large it should be, both the AI Act and the GDPR list factors to weigh. Which factors appear in both regimes?
gold: Both AIA Art. 99(7) and GDPR Art. 83(2) enumerate discretionary factors, and the following appear (in substance) in both, though phrased differently ('operator' in the AIA, 'controller or processor' in the GDPR): (1) the nature, gravity and duration of the infringement and its consequences, including the number of affected persons and the level of damage — AIA 99(7)(a) / GDPR 83(2)(a); (2) the intentional or negligent character of the infringement — AIA 99(7)(i) / GDPR 83(2)(b); (3) action taken by the operator/controller/processor to mitigate the harm or damage suffered — AIA 99(7)(j) / GDPR 83(2)(c); (4) the degree of responsibility taking into account the technical and organisational measures implemented — AIA 99(7)(g) / GDPR 83(2)(d); (5) the degree of cooperation with the competent/supervisory authority to remedy the infringement and mitigate adverse effects — AIA 99(7)(f) / GDPR 83(2)(f); (6) the manner in which the infringement became known to the authority, in particular whether and to what extent the operator/controller/processor notified it — AIA 99(7)(h) / GDPR 83(2)(h); and (7) any other aggravating or mitigating factor, such as financial benefits gained or losses avoided directly or indirectly from the infringement — AIA 99(7)(e) / GDPR 83(2)(k). [Factors that are NOT clean cross-regime matches — e.g. AIA 99(7)(b)/(c) on prior fines by other authorities vs GDPR 83(2)(e) on previous infringements, and GDPR-only items such as 83(2)(g) categories of personal data and 83(2)(j) adherence to codes of conduct/certification — are neither required for a correct answer nor penalised if included with a correct caveat.]
grading_rule: correct requires identifying the overlapping factors by MEANING across both lists (not by matching wording), citing a retrieved aia-art99-para7 AND a retrieved gdpr-art83-para2. The accepted overlap set is the seven enumerated in the gold: nature/gravity/duration+consequences; intentional/negligent character; mitigation action; degree of responsibility re technical+organisational measures; cooperation with the authority; manner of becoming known / self-notification; and other aggravating/mitigating incl. financial benefit. A correct answer names at least five of these seven with both-side attribution. Naming fewer than five is partial. Asserting an overlap that does not hold (e.g. GDPR-only 'categories of personal data' as shared) is a factual error but is NOT wrong on its own unless it displaces the required matches — treat as partial. Missing citation to either side is partial. Citation to a non-retrieved chunk is wrong. Extras from the bracketed near-miss set are neither required nor penalised.

question: A deployer of a high-risk AI system fails to meet its Article 26 obligations. Which penalty applies?
gold: Under AIA Art. 99(4), non-compliance with the obligations of deployers pursuant to Article 26 — listed at Art. 99(4)(e) — is subject to administrative fines of up to EUR 15 000 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 3 % of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher. This is the AI Act's middle penalty tier, below the EUR 35 000 000 / 7 % ceiling reserved for the prohibited practices of Article 5. [Note: for SMEs and start-ups, Art. 99(6) caps this at whichever of the amount or percentage is LOWER. The content of the Article 26 obligations themselves is not asserted here beyond their identity as deployer obligations.]

question: Under the AI Act, how are administrative fines calculated for SMEs and start-ups?
gold: Under AIA Art. 99(6), in the case of SMEs, including start-ups, each fine referred to in Article 99 shall be up to the percentages or amount referred to in paragraphs 3, 4 and 5, whichever thereof is LOWER. This inverts the general rule applied to undertakings in paragraphs 3, 4 and 5, where the fine is the higher of the fixed amount or the turnover percentage.
grading_rule: correct requires stating the whichever-is-LOWER rule for SMEs/start-ups, cited to a retrieved aia-art99-para6. Stating 'whichever is higher' for SMEs is wrong (that is the general/undertaking rule). Omitting that it references the ceilings in paragraphs 3, 4 and 5 is partial. Correct rule cited to a non-retrieved chunk is wrong.

question: Under the GDPR, when an undertaking faces a fine, is it calculated as the lower of the fixed amount and the turnover percentage?
gold: REFUSE (premise is wrong): No. Under GDPR Art. 83(5), for an undertaking the fine is up to EUR 20 000 000 or up to 4 % of total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding financial year, WHICHEVER IS HIGHER — not the lower of the two. The 'whichever is lower' formula belongs to a different regime: it is the AI Act's rule for SMEs and start-ups under AIA Art. 99(6), and does not apply to undertakings under the GDPR. The correct GDPR rule for an undertaking is the higher of the fixed amount or the turnover percentage.

Accepting the premise and describing GDPR fines as 'whichever is lower' is wrong. Note this row DOES require a citation (unlike an out-of-scope refusal): the correct answer is grounded in retrieved GDPR text, so an uncited correct rejection is partial. question: Which categories of infringement fall under the GDPR's highest fine tier?
gold: The GDPR's highest tier — up to EUR 20 000 000 or, for an undertaking, up to 4 % of total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding financial year, whichever is higher — is set by Art. 83(5) and Art. 83(6). Under Art. 83(5) it covers: (a) the basic principles for processing, including conditions for consent, pursuant to Articles 5, 6, 7 and 9; (b) the data subjects' rights pursuant to Articles 12 to 22; (c) transfers of personal data to a recipient in a third country or an international organisation pursuant to Articles 44 to 49; (d) any obligations pursuant to Member State law adopted under Chapter IX; and (e) non-compliance with an order or a temporary or definitive limitation on processing or suspension of data flows by the supervisory authority pursuant to Article 58(2), or failure to provide access in violation of Article 58(1). Under Art. 83(6), it also covers non-compliance with an order by the supervisory authority as referred to in Article 58(2). [The referenced articles (5, 6, 7, 9, 12-22, 44-49, 58) are named as cross-references; their substantive content is outside the pasted text.]

question: Under the GDPR, how quickly must a controller notify a personal data breach to the supervisory authority, and is there a case where no notification is required?
gold: Without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after having become aware of it (Art. 33(1)). No notification is required where the breach is unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons. A notification made later than 72 hours must be accompanied by reasons for the delay.
grading_rule: Must state 72 hours AND the 'unlikely to result in a risk' carve-out. '72 hours' with no exception is partial - the exception is what makes the rule operable. Stating 72 hours as an absolute deadline with no 'without undue delay' framing is partial, not wrong.

question: What right does the GDPR give a data subject in relation to decisions based solely on automated processing, and when does that right not apply?
gold: The right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling, which produces legal effects concerning him or her or similarly significantly affects him or her (Art. 22(1)). Art. 22(2) disapplies it where the decision is necessary for entering into or performing a contract, is authorised by Union or Member State law laying down suitable safeguards, or is based on the data subject's explicit consent.
grading_rule: Must keep the word 'solely' and the legal-effects / similarly-significantly threshold; dropping 'solely' is wrong, not partial, because it changes which systems are in scope. Stating the right with no mention of the Art. 22(2) exceptions is partial, on the same reasoning as sh-003.

question: Under what conditions does the GDPR right to data portability apply, and in what form must the data be provided?
gold: It applies where the processing is based on consent (Art. 6(1)(a) or Art. 9(2)(a)) or on a contract (Art. 6(1)(b)), and is carried out by automated means. The data subject has the right to receive the personal data he or she provided to the controller in a structured, commonly used and machine-readable format, and to transmit it to another controller without hindrance (Art. 20(1)).
grading_rule: Must name both conditions (consent-or-contract AND automated means) and the structured/commonly used/machine-readable format. Giving the format but not the two conditions is partial - the conditions are what bound the right.

question: On what grounds can a data subject obtain erasure of personal data under the GDPR?
gold: Art. 17(1) lists six grounds: the data are no longer necessary for the purposes for which they were collected; the data subject withdraws the consent the processing rests on and there is no other legal ground; the data subject objects under Art. 21(1) and there are no overriding legitimate grounds, or objects under Art. 21(2); the data have been unlawfully processed; erasure is required for compliance with a Union or Member State legal obligation; or the data were collected in relation to information society services offered to a child under Art. 8(1). Where a ground applies the controller must erase without undue delay.
grading_rule: Must convey that erasure is ground-conditional, not on demand, and name at least three of the six grounds. Presenting erasure as an unconditional right is wrong, not partial.

question: When is a data protection impact assessment required under the GDPR?
gold: Where a type of processing, in particular using new technologies and taking into account its nature, scope, context and purposes, is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons, the controller must carry out a DPIA prior to the processing (Art. 35(1)). Art. 35(3) makes it required in particular for systematic and extensive automated evaluation producing legal or similarly significant effects, large-scale processing of Art. 9(1) special categories or Art. 10 criminal-conviction data, and systematic monitoring of a publicly accessible area on a large scale.
grading_rule: Must state the 'likely to result in a high risk' trigger and that the assessment is prior to processing. Listing the Art. 35(3) cases as the only triggers is partial - they are examples, not the test.

question: In which cases must a controller or processor designate a data protection officer under the GDPR?
gold: In three cases (Art. 37(1)): where processing is carried out by a public authority or body, except courts acting in their judicial capacity; where the core activities require regular and systematic monitoring of data subjects on a large scale; or where the core activities consist of large-scale processing of Art. 9 special categories or Art. 10 criminal-conviction data.
grading_rule: Must name all three cases and keep the 'core activities' and 'large scale' qualifiers. Dropping 'core activities' is partial - it is the qualifier that keeps incidental processing out of scope.

question: What does data protection by default require of a controller under the GDPR?
gold: That the controller implement appropriate technical and organisational measures ensuring that, by default, only personal data necessary for each specific purpose of the processing are processed (Art. 25(2)). The obligation covers the amount of data collected, the extent of processing, the storage period and accessibility, and the measures must in particular ensure that personal data are not by default made accessible to an indefinite number of natural persons without the individual's intervention.
grading_rule: Must state the necessity-per-purpose default. Naming the four dimensions (amount, extent, storage period, accessibility) or the indefinite-number clause is a bonus. Answering about by-design (Art. 25(1)) instead of by-default is wrong - the question names the default limb.

question: How long does a controller have to respond to a data subject request under the GDPR, and can that period be extended?
gold: Without undue delay and in any event within one month of receipt of the request (Art. 12(3)). The period may be extended by two further months where necessary, taking into account the complexity and number of the requests, and the controller must inform the data subject of the extension within one month of receipt together with the reasons for the delay.
grading_rule: Must state one month AND the two-month extension. One month alone is partial. Stating any other base period is wrong.

question: What is a data subject entitled to obtain under the GDPR right of access?
gold: Confirmation as to whether personal data concerning him or her are being processed and, where that is the case, access to the personal data together with the information listed in Art. 15(1)(a)-(h): the purposes of processing, the categories of personal data, the recipients or categories of recipient, the envisaged storage period or the criteria for it, the existence of the rights to rectification, erasure, restriction and objection, the right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority, any available information on the source where the data were not collected from the data subject, and the existence of automated decision-making including profiling under Art. 22(1) and (4).
grading_rule: Must cover both limbs - the confirmation-of-processing limb and the access-plus-information limb - and name at least four of the eight information items. Treating access as a right to a copy of the data alone is partial.

question: Does the AI Act allow an employer to use an AI system that infers the emotions of its staff?
gold: No. Art. 5(1)(f) prohibits the placing on the market, putting into service for that specific purpose, or use of AI systems to infer emotions of a natural person in the areas of workplace and education institutions. The single exception is where the system is intended to be put in place or on the market for medical or safety reasons.
grading_rule: Must say prohibited AND name the medical-or-safety exception. A flat 'prohibited' with no exception is partial on the sh-003 reasoning. Classifying it as high-risk rather than prohibited is wrong - that is the Annex III treatment of emotion recognition outside the workplace and education.

question: Under the AI Act, must a provider tell people they are interacting with an AI system, and is there any exception?
gold: Yes. Providers must ensure that AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons are designed and developed so that the persons concerned are informed they are interacting with an AI system, unless this is obvious to a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person in the circumstances and context of use (Art. 50(1)). The obligation does not apply to AI systems authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences, subject to appropriate safeguards, unless the system is available for the public to report an offence.
grading_rule: Must state the disclosure duty and at least one of the two carve-outs (the obviousness carve-out or the law-enforcement carve-out). Naming neither is partial.

question: What does the AI Act require of providers of AI systems that generate synthetic audio, image, video or text content?
gold: That the outputs be marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated, with technical solutions that are effective, interoperable, robust and reliable as far as technically feasible (Art. 50(2)). This includes general-purpose AI systems. The obligation does not apply where the system performs an assistive function for standard editing or does not substantially alter the deployer's input data or its semantics, or where authorised by law for criminal-offence purposes.
grading_rule: Must state machine-readable marking and detectability as artificially generated. Describing it as a visible watermark or a user-facing label only is partial - the text says machine-readable.

question: What documentation obligations does the AI Act place on providers of general-purpose AI models?
gold: Under Art. 53(1) they must draw up and keep up to date the technical documentation of the model, including its training and testing process and evaluation results, containing at a minimum the information in Annex XI, for provision on request to the AI Office and national competent authorities; and draw up, keep up to date and make available information and documentation to downstream providers who intend to integrate the model, containing at a minimum the elements in Annex XII. They must also put in place a policy to comply with Union copyright law.
grading_rule: Must distinguish the two documentation duties - the Annex XI set held for the AI Office and authorities, and the Annex XII set made available to downstream providers. Merging them into one undifferentiated documentation duty is partial.

question: How does the AI Act define an 'emotion recognition system'?
gold: An AI system for the purpose of identifying or inferring emotions or intentions of natural persons on the basis of their biometric data (Art. 3(39)).
grading_rule: Must include the biometric-data basis and cover intentions as well as emotions. Omitting the biometric-data basis is wrong - it is what separates this from sentiment analysis over text.

question: An employer puts a high-risk AI system into use at the workplace. Whom must it inform beforehand, and what is the maximum administrative fine for failing that obligation?
gold: Before putting into service or using a high-risk AI system at the workplace, deployers who are employers must inform workers' representatives and the affected workers that they will be subject to its use (Art. 26(7)). Deployer obligations under Art. 26 fall in the Art. 99(4)(e) tier: fines up to EUR 15 000 000 or, for an undertaking, up to 3 % of total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher.
grading_rule: Must name both workers' representatives AND affected workers, and must give the 15M/3% tier with 'whichever is higher'. Giving 35M/7% is wrong - that is the Art. 5 prohibited-practices tier. 'Whichever is lower' is wrong; see hn-001.

question: A provider of a high-risk AI system fails to meet its Article 16 obligations. Which penalty tier applies and what is the ceiling?
gold: Art. 99(4)(a) covers obligations of providers pursuant to Art. 16, so the ceiling is EUR 15 000 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 3 % of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher. Art. 16 requires providers to ensure compliance with the Section 2 requirements, indicate their name and contact details on the system, operate a quality management system, keep documentation and logs, and take corrective action.
grading_rule: Must land on the 15M/3% tier and connect it to Art. 16 via Art. 99(4)(a). Naming the tier without identifying which Art. 99 paragraph routes Art. 16 there is partial.

question: A start-up breaches the AI Act's prohibition on certain AI practices. How does its SME status change the fine it faces?
gold: The general rule in Art. 99(3) for non-compliance with the Art. 5 prohibitions is up to EUR 35 000 000 or, for an undertaking, up to 7 % of total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher. For SMEs including start-ups, Art. 99(6) inverts that: each fine is up to the percentage or the amount referred to in paragraphs 3, 4 and 5, whichever is lower.
grading_rule: Must state the general higher-of rule AND the SME lower-of inversion. Giving only the 35M/7% figure is partial - the question is about the SME modifier. Saying SMEs are exempt is wrong.

question: A bank deploys an Annex III high-risk AI system that assists in credit decisions about individuals. What must it tell those individuals, and how does that sit with the AI Act's general transparency rule?
gold: Deployers of Annex III high-risk AI systems that make or assist in making decisions related to natural persons must inform those persons that they are subject to the use of the system (Art. 26(11)). That duty applies without prejudice to Art. 50, which separately requires providers to ensure that systems intended to interact directly with natural persons disclose that the person is interacting with an AI system - the two obligations stack rather than substitute.
grading_rule: Must state the Art. 26(11) deployer duty and that it is without prejudice to Art. 50. Treating Art. 50 as discharging the Art. 26(11) duty is wrong - 'without prejudice' means both apply.

question: Which providers must register a high-risk AI system before placing it on the market, and in which database?
gold: Before placing on the market or putting into service a high-risk AI system listed in Annex III - except systems referred to in point 2 of Annex III - the provider or, where applicable, the authorised representative must register themselves and their system in the EU database referred to in Art. 71 (Art. 49(1)). That database is set up and maintained by the Commission in collaboration with the Member States (Art. 71(1)).
grading_rule: Must name the EU database under Art. 71 and the point 2 of Annex III exception. Omitting the exception is partial; naming a national register instead of the EU database is wrong.

question: Which deployers of high-risk AI systems must carry out a fundamental rights impact assessment, and which systems are carved out?
gold: Deployers that are bodies governed by public law or private entities providing public services, and deployers of high-risk systems referred to in points 5(b) and (c) of Annex III, must perform a FRIA prior to deploying a high-risk system referred to in Art. 6(2) (Art. 27(1)). Systems intended to be used in the area listed in point 2 of Annex III are excepted. Art. 6(2) is the limb that makes Annex III systems high-risk in the first place.
grading_rule: Must identify both categories of deployer (public-law bodies / private providers of public services, and Annex III 5(b)-(c) deployers) and the point 2 carve-out. Saying every deployer of a high-risk system must do a FRIA is wrong - it is the error the article's opening clause exists to prevent.

question: A controller refuses to answer subject access requests. Which GDPR fine tier does that fall into, and what is the ceiling?
gold: Art. 15(1) gives the data subject the right of access. Infringements of the data subjects' rights under Arts. 12 to 22 fall under Art. 83(5)(b), which carries administrative fines up to EUR 20 000 000 or, in the case of an undertaking, up to 4 % of total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding financial year, whichever is higher.
grading_rule: Must give the 20M/4% tier and route it via the Arts. 12-22 data-subject-rights limb of Art. 83(5). Giving the 10M/2% tier is wrong - that is Art. 83(4), the controller/processor-obligations tier.

question: A controller has implemented no data protection by design measures at all. Which GDPR fine tier applies?
gold: Art. 25 requires the controller to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures, such as pseudonymisation, designed to implement data-protection principles and integrate the necessary safeguards. Art. 83(4)(a) covers the obligations of the controller and processor pursuant to Arts. 8, 11, 25 to 39 and 42 and 43, so the ceiling is EUR 10 000 000 or, for an undertaking, up to 2 % of total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding financial year, whichever is higher.
grading_rule: Must give the 10M/2% tier and connect Art. 25 to it through the Arts. 25-39 enumeration in Art. 83(4)(a). Giving 20M/4% is wrong. This row and th-011 are a matched pair: a system that gives the same tier for both has not read the enumeration.

question: There is no Commission adequacy decision for the third country a controller wants to send personal data to. On what basis may the transfer still go ahead?
gold: An adequacy decision under Art. 45(1) would let the transfer proceed without any specific authorisation. In its absence, Art. 46(1) allows a controller or processor to transfer only if it has provided appropriate safeguards and on condition that enforceable data subject rights and effective legal remedies are available to data subjects.
grading_rule: Must state the appropriate-safeguards route AND both attached conditions (enforceable rights and effective remedies). Naming safeguards without the conditions is partial - the conditions are the operative test.

question: What must a controller-processor contract stipulate under the GDPR, and what is the exposure if there is no such contract?
gold: Processing by a processor must be governed by a binding contract or other legal act setting out the subject-matter and duration, the nature and purpose of the processing, the type of personal data and categories of data subjects, and the controller's obligations and rights; it must in particular stipulate that the processor processes only on documented instructions, ensures confidentiality commitments from authorised persons, and takes the Art. 32 security measures (Art. 28(3)). Art. 28 falls inside the Arts. 25 to 39 enumeration in Art. 83(4)(a), so the ceiling is EUR 10 000 000 or up to 2 % of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher.
grading_rule: Must name at least three required contract terms and land on the 10M/2% tier. Giving the 20M/4% tier is wrong.

question: A provider believes its Annex III AI system is not high-risk. What is the default classification and what must the provider do to act on that view?
gold: By default, AI systems referred to in Annex III are considered high-risk (Art. 6(2)). A provider who considers that such a system is not high-risk must document its assessment before the system is placed on the market or put into service, is still subject to the registration obligation in Art. 49(2), and must provide the documentation of the assessment on request of national competent authorities (Art. 6(4)).
grading_rule: Must state that Annex III listing makes a system high-risk by default and that the derogation is documented and self-assessed, not granted. Must keep the residual registration obligation; dropping it is partial, because 'not high-risk therefore nothing to do' is the misreading this paragraph exists to block.

question: What must a deployer of an emotion recognition system do, and what counts as such a system under the AI Act?
gold: An emotion recognition system is an AI system for the purpose of identifying or inferring emotions or intentions of natural persons on the basis of their biometric data (Art. 3(39)). Deployers of such a system, or of a biometric categorisation system, must inform the natural persons exposed to it of the operation of the system and must process the personal data in accordance with the applicable data-protection law (Art. 50(3)).
grading_rule: Must give the biometric-data basis from the definition and the deployer information duty. An answer that only quotes the definition, or only the duty, is partial - the question asks for the link between them.

question: Are open-source general-purpose AI model providers exempt from the AI Act's model documentation obligations?
gold: Partly. Art. 53(1)(a) and (b) impose the technical-documentation and downstream-information duties. Art. 53(2) disapplies those two points for providers of AI models released under a free and open-source licence allowing access, usage, modification and distribution, whose parameters including weights, model architecture information and model usage information are made publicly available. The exception does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk, and it does not touch the Art. 53(1)(c) copyright-policy duty.
grading_rule: Must state that the exemption is limited to points (a) and (b) AND that it falls away for models with systemic risk. A flat 'yes, open-source is exempt' is wrong. Missing the systemic-risk carve-back is partial.

question: A DPIA shows that a planned processing operation would result in a high risk. What must the controller do next under the GDPR?
gold: Where a DPIA under Art. 35 indicates that the processing would result in a high risk in the absence of measures taken by the controller to mitigate the risk, the controller must consult the supervisory authority prior to processing (Art. 36(1)). The DPIA itself is required where a type of processing, in particular using new technologies, is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons (Art. 35(1)).
grading_rule: Must reach prior consultation with the supervisory authority. Must keep the mitigation qualifier - consultation is triggered by residual high risk after mitigation, so 'any DPIA showing high risk requires consultation' is partial.

question: After a personal data breach, when must a controller tell the supervisory authority and when must it tell the affected individuals?
gold: The supervisory authority must be notified without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of becoming aware, unless the breach is unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons (Art. 33(1)). The data subjects must be told only where the breach is likely to result in a *high* risk to their rights and freedoms, and then without undue delay (Art. 34(1)).
grading_rule: Must distinguish the two thresholds: 'risk' for the authority, 'high risk' for the data subject. Applying the 72-hour clock to the data-subject communication is wrong - Art. 34(1) sets no such deadline. Collapsing the two thresholds into one is wrong.

question: What ongoing monitoring must a provider of a high-risk AI system run after the system is on the market, and to whom does it report a serious incident?
gold: Providers must establish and document a post-market monitoring system proportionate to the nature of the AI technologies and the risks of the high-risk AI system (Art. 72(1)). Providers of high-risk AI systems placed on the Union market must report any serious incident to the market surveillance authorities of the Member States where the incident occurred (Art. 73(1)).
grading_rule: Must name market surveillance authorities of the Member State where the incident occurred as the recipient. Naming the AI Office or the Commission as the primary recipient is wrong. Must cover both limbs - monitoring system and incident reporting.

question: A company builds an AI system that filters job applications. Which conformity assessment procedure must it follow before placing the system on the market, and is a notified body involved?
gold: Recruitment and selection systems, including systems to analyse and filter job applications, are listed in point 4 of Annex III. AI systems referred to in Annex III are considered high-risk (Art. 6(2)). For high-risk systems in points 2 to 8 of Annex III, the provider must follow the conformity assessment procedure based on internal control referred to in Annex VI, which does not provide for the involvement of a notified body (Art. 43(2)).
grading_rule: Must reach internal control / Annex VI AND state that no notified body is involved. Requiring a notified body is wrong - that is the point 1 (biometrics) route under Art. 43(1). Must place the system in Annex III point 4 to get there; landing on the right answer without the classification step is partial.

question: A municipality wants to use an AI system to decide eligibility for social assistance benefits. Must it carry out a fundamental rights impact assessment before deploying it?
gold: Yes. AI systems intended to be used by public authorities to evaluate eligibility for essential public assistance benefits and services, including to grant, reduce, revoke or reclaim them, are listed in point 5(a) of Annex III, and Annex III systems are high-risk under Art. 6(2). Art. 27(1) requires deployers that are bodies governed by public law to perform a fundamental rights impact assessment prior to deploying a high-risk system referred to in Art. 6(2). The point 2 of Annex III carve-out does not apply here.
grading_rule: Must answer yes and reach Art. 27(1) through the public-law-body limb. An answer that says yes because 'it is high-risk' without identifying the deployer category is partial - Art. 27 does not apply to every deployer of every high-risk system.

question: An employer deploys an AI system to evaluate candidates for promotion without telling anyone. What obligation has it breached and what is the maximum fine?
gold: Systems used to make decisions affecting terms of work-related relationships, including promotion, are in point 4 of Annex III and are therefore high-risk. Art. 26(7) requires deployers who are employers to inform workers' representatives and the affected workers before putting a high-risk AI system into use at the workplace. Deployer obligations under Art. 26 are penalised under Art. 99(4)(e): up to EUR 15 000 000 or, for an undertaking, 3 % of total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher.
grading_rule: Must identify the Art. 26(7) information duty and the 15M/3% tier. Giving 35M/7% is wrong. Naming only the affected workers and not their representatives is partial.

question: A vendor sells a remote biometric identification system in the EU. How does its conformity assessment route differ from that of other Annex III systems?
gold: Remote biometric identification systems are in point 1 of Annex III, and Annex III systems are high-risk under Art. 6(2). For high-risk systems listed in point 1 of Annex III, Art. 43(1) requires the provider to choose between conformity assessment routes that include notified-body involvement, where the provider has applied harmonised standards or common specifications. Every other Annex III category - points 2 to 8 - follows internal control under Annex VI with no notified body (Art. 43(2)).
grading_rule: Must draw the point 1 versus points 2-8 distinction. Saying every Annex III system needs a notified body is wrong; saying none does is also wrong. This row is the mirror of 3h-003 and sh-002 - a system that gives the same answer to all three has collapsed the distinction.

question: A university uses an AI system to decide admissions. What does the AI Act require regarding human oversight, both of the system and of the university as deployer?
gold: Systems used to determine access or admission to educational and vocational training institutions are in point 3 of Annex III and are high-risk. Art. 14(1) requires the high-risk AI system itself to be designed and developed so that it can be effectively overseen by natural persons during use, including through appropriate human-machine interface tools. Art. 26(2) puts a matching duty on the deployer: it must assign human oversight to natural persons who have the necessary competence, training and authority, as well as the necessary support.
grading_rule: Must cover both limbs - the design duty on the provider under Art. 14 and the assignment duty on the deployer under Art. 26(2), including competence/training/authority/support. Covering only one limb is partial.

question: A court uses an AI system to help interpret facts and law. What transparency must the system provide, and what must the court do with the information it receives?
gold: AI systems used by a judicial authority to assist in researching and interpreting facts and the law are in point 8 of Annex III and are high-risk. Art. 13(1) requires high-risk AI systems to be designed and developed so that their operation is sufficiently transparent to enable deployers to interpret the output and use it appropriately. Art. 26(9) requires the deployer, where applicable, to use the information provided under Art. 13 to comply with its obligation to carry out a data protection impact assessment under Art. 35 GDPR or Art. 27 of Directive (EU) 2016/680.
grading_rule: Must connect Art. 13 transparency to the Art. 26(9) downstream use of that information for a DPIA. Describing Art. 13 transparency alone is partial - the second half of the question is the onward duty.

question: An insurer plans large-scale processing of health data. What assessment must it run, what must it do if the risk stays high, and what does it risk if it does neither?
gold: Processing on a large scale of special categories of data referred to in Art. 9(1) - which includes health data - requires a data protection impact assessment under Art. 35(3)(b). Where the DPIA indicates that the processing would result in a high risk absent mitigating measures, the controller must consult the supervisory authority prior to processing (Art. 36(1)). Arts. 35 and 36 sit inside the Arts. 25 to 39 enumeration in Art. 83(4)(a), so the exposure is up to EUR 10 000 000 or, for an undertaking, 2 % of total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding financial year, whichever is higher.
grading_rule: Must reach all three steps: DPIA required, prior consultation on residual high risk, 10M/2% tier. Giving the 20M/4% tier is wrong - Arts. 35-36 are Art. 83(4) obligations, not Art. 83(5) rights or principles.

question: A lender makes fully automated credit decisions by profiling applicants. Which GDPR right is engaged, what assessment is required, and what fine tier applies to breaching that right?
gold: Art. 22(1) gives the data subject the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling, which produces legal effects or similarly significantly affects him or her. A systematic and extensive evaluation of personal aspects based on automated processing, including profiling, on which such decisions are based, requires a DPIA under Art. 35(3)(a). Infringements of data subjects' rights under Arts. 12 to 22 fall under Art. 83(5)(b): up to EUR 20 000 000 or, for an undertaking, 4 % of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher.
grading_rule: Must reach the 20M/4% tier via the Arts. 12-22 limb. Pairs with 3h-009: same shape, opposite tier. A system that gives both rows the same ceiling has not read the Art. 83 enumerations.

question: Who enforces deployer obligations under the AI Act at national level, what must the deployer do when they act, and who sets the penalties?
gold: Each Member State must establish or designate at least one notifying authority and at least one market surveillance authority as national competent authorities, exercising their powers independently and impartially (Art. 70(1)). Deployers must cooperate with the relevant competent authorities in any action those authorities take in relation to the high-risk AI system in order to implement the Regulation (Art. 26(12)). The rules on penalties and other enforcement measures, which may include warnings and non-monetary measures, are laid down by the Member States (Art. 99(1)).
grading_rule: Must name the market surveillance authority as the national enforcer and Member States as the source of the penalty rules. Naming the Commission or the AI Office as the national enforcer of deployer obligations is wrong.

question: A general-purpose AI model provider must hold technical documentation for the AI Office. Where is the required content specified and what does it have to include?
gold: Art. 53(1)(a) requires providers of general-purpose AI models to draw up and keep up to date the technical documentation of the model, including its training and testing process and evaluation results, containing at a minimum the information set out in Annex XI, for provision on request to the AI Office and national competent authorities. Annex XI Section 1 requires, among other things, a general description of the model covering the tasks it is intended to perform and the type of AI systems it can be integrated into, the acceptable use policies, the date of release and methods of distribution, and the architecture and number of parameters.
grading_rule: Must name Annex XI as the source of the required content and the AI Office as a recipient on request, and give at least two concrete Annex XI Section 1 items. Naming Annex XII is wrong - that is the downstream-provider set under Art. 53(1)(b).

question: A five-person start-up markets an AI system that infers employees' emotions at work. What has it done wrong and what is its maximum exposure?
gold: Art. 5(1)(f) prohibits placing on the market, putting into service for that specific purpose, or using AI systems to infer emotions of a natural person in the areas of workplace and education institutions, except for medical or safety reasons. Non-compliance with the Art. 5 prohibitions carries administrative fines up to EUR 35 000 000 or, for an undertaking, up to 7 % of total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher (Art. 99(3)). Because it is an SME, Art. 99(6) applies each such fine up to the percentage or the amount, whichever is lower.
grading_rule: Must reach the prohibition (not high-risk classification), the 35M/7% tier, and the SME lower-of inversion. Missing the SME inversion is partial; classifying the practice as high-risk rather than prohibited is wrong.

question: A controller transfers personal data to a third country with no adequacy decision and no safeguards in place. Which route should it have used and what is the fine exposure?
gold: With an adequacy decision the transfer could have proceeded with no specific authorisation (Art. 45(1)). Absent one, Art. 46(1) permits the transfer only where the controller or processor has provided appropriate safeguards and enforceable data subject rights and effective legal remedies are available. Transfers to a recipient in a third country or international organisation pursuant to Arts. 44 to 49 fall under Art. 83(5)(c): up to EUR 20 000 000 or, for an undertaking, 4 % of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher.
grading_rule: Must reach the 20M/4% tier via the Arts. 44-49 transfers limb of Art. 83(5)(c). Giving the 10M/2% tier is wrong. Must state the safeguards route with its two attached conditions.

question: Is a biometric categorisation system prohibited under the AI Act or merely high-risk?
gold: It depends on what it categorises by. Art. 5(1)(g) prohibits biometric categorisation systems that categorise individually natural persons based on their biometric data to deduce or infer race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation. Biometric categorisation according to sensitive or protected attributes otherwise appears in point 1(b) of Annex III, and Annex III systems are high-risk under Art. 6(2). So the same technology sits in different tiers depending on the inferred attribute.
grading_rule: Must state that both tiers exist and that the inferred attribute is what separates them. Answering flatly 'prohibited' or flatly 'high-risk' is wrong - the question is built on the distinction, and a single-tier answer is the failure mode being probed.

question: What does the UK Online Safety Act require of providers of AI chatbots?
gold: REFUSE: the corpus covers the EU AI Act and GDPR only. UK legislation is not ingested, and no answer or citation should be produced.
grading_rule: correct-refusal = declines and names the scope limit, with ZERO fabricated citations. wrong = any substantive answer or any citation. The near-miss here is answering from AIA Art. 50 transparency rules as though they were UK law - that is wrong, not partial, because it misattributes a provision to the wrong instrument.

question: Under the Digital Services Act, what must very large online platforms do about their recommender systems?
gold: REFUSE: the corpus covers Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act) and Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR) only. The Digital Services Act is not ingested.
grading_rule: correct-refusal = declines and names the scope limit, with ZERO fabricated citations. wrong = any substantive answer or any citation. Harder than oos-003 because the DSA is EU law and adjacent in subject matter: a system that refuses US law but answers on the DSA is drawing the boundary at 'EU' rather than at 'ingested', which is the distinction this row tests.

question: What labelling does China's deep synthesis regulation require for AI-generated content?

question: The GDPR gives data subjects an absolute right to have their data deleted on request - can you confirm a controller must always comply?
gold: REFUSE (premise is wrong): No, the right to erasure is not absolute. Art. 17(1) makes it conditional: the controller must erase without undue delay only where one of six listed grounds applies - the data are no longer necessary for the purposes; consent is withdrawn and no other legal ground exists; the data subject objects under Art. 21(1) with no overriding legitimate grounds, or objects under Art. 21(2); the data were unlawfully processed; erasure is required by a Union or Member State legal obligation; or the data were collected in relation to information society services offered to a child under Art. 8(1).

question: Since GDPR Article 22 bans automated decision-making, does a company need to stop using any algorithm that scores customers?
gold: REFUSE (premise is wrong): Art. 22 does not ban automated decision-making. Art. 22(1) gives the data subject a right not to be subject to a decision based SOLELY on automated processing, including profiling, which produces legal effects or similarly significantly affects him or her - so decisions with meaningful human involvement, or without legal or similarly significant effect, fall outside it. Art. 22(2) further disapplies the right where the decision is necessary for a contract, is authorised by Union or Member State law with suitable safeguards, or rests on explicit consent.
grading_rule: correct rejects the framing of Art. 22 as a ban and identifies BOTH limiters - the word 'solely' and the legal/similarly-significant-effects threshold - cited to retrieved text. Naming the Art. 22(2) exceptions as well is a bonus. Accepting 'Article 22 bans automated decision-making' is wrong.

question: Every high-risk AI system under Annex III has to be certified by a notified body before it goes on the market, correct?
gold: REFUSE (premise is wrong): No. For high-risk AI systems referred to in points 2 to 8 of Annex III, providers follow the conformity assessment procedure based on internal control referred to in Annex VI, which does not provide for the involvement of a notified body (Art. 43(2)). Notified-body involvement is the exception, arising for point 1 (biometrics) systems, not the rule across Annex III.
grading_rule: correct rejects the premise and identifies internal control / Annex VI for points 2 to 8, cited to a retrieved chunk. Confirming that all Annex III systems need a notified body is wrong. This is the inverse of sh-002 and 3h-006: a system that answers those correctly and still confirms this premise is agreeing with the user rather than with the text.

question: We had a personal data breach 60 hours ago. We still have 12 hours to tell the affected customers, right?
gold: REFUSE (premise is wrong): the 72-hour clock is not the deadline for telling data subjects. Art. 33(1) sets 72 hours for notifying the SUPERVISORY AUTHORITY, without undue delay and where feasible, unless the breach is unlikely to result in a risk. Communication to the data subject is governed by Art. 34(1), which applies only where the breach is likely to result in a HIGH risk to their rights and freedoms, and requires it without undue delay - it attaches no 72-hour allowance.
grading_rule: correct rejects the premise by separating the two duties and their two thresholds (risk vs high risk), cited to retrieved text. Confirming that 12 hours remain to notify customers is wrong. Naming the 72 hours without correcting which duty it attaches to is wrong, not partial - the premise survives.

question: Our general-purpose model is open source, so the AI Act does not apply to us at all - can you confirm?
gold: REFUSE (premise is wrong): the open-source carve-out is narrow. Art. 53(2) disapplies only Art. 53(1) points (a) and (b) - the technical documentation and downstream-information duties - and only for models released under a free and open-source licence permitting access, usage, modification and distribution whose parameters, including weights, architecture information and usage information, are publicly available. The exception does not apply at all to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk, and it does not touch the Art. 53(1)(c) duty to have a Union copyright compliance policy.
grading_rule: correct rejects 'does not apply at all' and states the two boundaries: only points (a) and (b), and never for systemic-risk models. Confirming blanket exemption is wrong. Stating the carve-out without the systemic-risk carve-back is partial.

question: Annex III is just an indicative list, so we can simply declare our recruitment system is not high-risk and move on?
gold: REFUSE (premise is wrong): Annex III is not indicative. Art. 6(2) provides that AI systems referred to in Annex III shall be considered to be high-risk. A provider who considers such a system not to be high-risk must document its assessment before the system is placed on the market or put into service, remains subject to the registration obligation in Art. 49(2), and must provide the documentation to national competent authorities on request (Art. 6(4)). The default is high-risk and the departure is a documented, auditable position - not a declaration.
grading_rule: correct rejects 'indicative' and 'simply declare', and keeps the residual registration and documentation duties. Confirming that a provider may self-declare out with no further obligation is wrong. Rejecting the premise but dropping the surviving Art. 49(2) registration duty is partial.

question: The GDPR requires a data protection impact assessment for every processing operation involving personal data, doesn't it?
gold: REFUSE (premise is wrong): No. Art. 35(1) requires a DPIA only where a type of processing, in particular using new technologies and taking into account its nature, scope, context and purposes, is LIKELY TO RESULT IN A HIGH RISK to the rights and freedoms of natural persons; it must then be carried out prior to the processing. A single assessment may cover a set of similar processing operations presenting similar high risks. Processing that does not meet the high-risk threshold requires no DPIA.
grading_rule: correct rejects the universality premise and states the likely-high-risk trigger, cited to a retrieved chunk. Confirming that every processing operation needs a DPIA is wrong. Note the tension with sh-011, which asks the same provision straight: a system that gets sh-011 right and hn-009 wrong is agreeing with the questioner rather than reading.

question: We are on day 29 of a subject access request and cannot finish in time. We have missed the deadline and are automatically in breach, correct?
gold: REFUSE (premise is wrong): not necessarily. Art. 12(3) requires the controller to provide information on action taken without undue delay and in any event within one month of receipt. That period may be extended by two further months where necessary, taking into account the complexity and number of the requests, provided the controller informs the data subject of the extension, together with the reasons for the delay, within one month of receipt of the request. Acting on day 29 to notify an extension is within the mechanism the Article provides.
grading_rule: correct rejects the automatic-breach premise and identifies the two-month extension AND its condition (notify within the original month, with reasons). Confirming automatic breach is wrong. Naming the extension without its notification condition is partial - the condition is what makes it available on day 29.

question: Can a provider of a high-risk AI system process special categories of personal data to test its model for bias, given that the GDPR prohibits such processing?
gold: Yes, exceptionally. GDPR Art. 9(1) prohibits processing of special categories of personal data by default. AIA Art. 10(5) permits providers of high-risk AI systems to process such data to the extent strictly necessary for bias detection and correction under Art. 10(2)(f) and (g), subject to appropriate safeguards. That permission is additional to - not instead of - the provisions of Regulation (EU) 2016/679, and is conditional on all the listed conditions being met: bias detection cannot be effectively achieved with other data including synthetic or anonymised data; technical limits on re-use plus state-of-the-art security and privacy-preserving measures including pseudonymisation; and strict access controls and documentation.
grading_rule: Must state that the AIA permission operates in addition to the GDPR rather than displacing it, and name at least two of the Art. 10(5) conditions. Presenting AIA Art. 10(5) as an exemption from the GDPR is wrong - the text says 'in addition to the provisions set out in Regulations (EU) 2016/679'.

question: We already did a GDPR data protection impact assessment for this high-risk AI system. Does that discharge the AI Act's fundamental rights impact assessment?
gold: No, it complements it. AIA Art. 27(4) provides that if any of the Art. 27 obligations is already met through the data protection impact assessment conducted under Art. 35 GDPR or Art. 27 of Directive (EU) 2016/680, the fundamental rights impact assessment shall COMPLEMENT that data protection impact assessment. The DPIA itself is required where processing is likely to result in a high risk to rights and freedoms (GDPR Art. 35(1)). So overlapping work need not be repeated, but the FRIA is not discharged by the DPIA.
grading_rule: Must use the word complement or convey that the FRIA survives alongside the DPIA. Answering that the DPIA satisfies the FRIA obligation is wrong. Answering that the two are entirely separate with no interaction is partial - Art. 27(4) exists precisely to allow reuse.

question: Does the AI Act override the GDPR where the two overlap?
gold: No. AIA Art. 2(7) provides that Union law on the protection of personal data, privacy and the confidentiality of communications applies to personal data processed in connection with the rights and obligations laid down in the AI Act, and that the AI Act shall not affect Regulation (EU) 2016/679 or (EU) 2018/1725, or Directive 2002/58/EC or (EU) 2016/680. The only reservations are Art. 10(5) and Art. 59 of the AI Act, which create narrow, conditioned processing permissions rather than a general override.
grading_rule: Must answer no and name the two reserved provisions (Art. 10(5) and Art. 59) or at least state that narrow exceptions exist. A flat 'no, the GDPR always applies' with no mention of the reservations is partial. Answering that the AI Act is lex specialis and prevails is wrong.

question: Can personal data collected for another purpose be reused to train an AI system in a regulatory sandbox, given the GDPR's purpose limitation principle?
gold: Yes, under conditions. GDPR Art. 5(1)(b) requires personal data to be collected for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes and not further processed in a manner incompatible with those purposes. AIA Art. 59(1) permits personal data lawfully collected for other purposes to be processed in the AI regulatory sandbox solely for developing, training and testing certain AI systems, when all listed conditions are met - including that the systems safeguard a substantial public interest in a named area such as public safety and health, environmental protection, energy sustainability, transport safety, or the efficiency of public administration, and that the data are necessary for meeting a Chapter III Section 2 requirement that anonymised or synthetic data cannot effectively fulfil.
grading_rule: Must state that this is a conditioned carve-out inside the sandbox, and name the substantial-public-interest requirement and at least one listed area. Presenting sandbox reuse as unconditional is wrong. Answering that purpose limitation forbids it outright is wrong.

question: Which authority does market surveillance for a biometric identification system used by police, and how does that relate to the data protection supervisory authority?
gold: They can be the same body. AIA Art. 74(8) requires Member States to designate, for high-risk AI systems listed in point 1 of Annex III in so far as they are used for law enforcement, border management, justice and democracy, and for those in points 6, 7 and 8 of Annex III, either the competent data protection supervisory authorities under Regulation (EU) 2016/679 or Directive (EU) 2016/680, or another authority designated under the same conditions in Arts. 41 to 44 of Directive (EU) 2016/680. Under GDPR Art. 51(1) each Member State provides for one or more independent public authorities as supervisory authority. Market surveillance activities must in no way affect the independence of judicial authorities.
grading_rule: Must identify that the DPA may be designated as the market surveillance authority for these categories. Naming a generic market surveillance authority with no connection to the data protection supervisory authority is partial - the designation link is the whole point of the question.

question: How does the information a deployer receives from the provider of a high-risk AI system feed into its GDPR obligations?
gold: AIA Art. 26(9) requires deployers of high-risk AI systems, where applicable, to use the information provided under AIA Art. 13 to comply with their obligation to carry out a data protection impact assessment under Art. 35 GDPR or Art. 27 of Directive (EU) 2016/680. Art. 13 is the provider-side transparency requirement that makes the system's operation sufficiently transparent for the deployer to interpret its output and use it appropriately, and Art. 35(1) GDPR is what triggers the DPIA where processing is likely to result in a high risk.

question: A retailer deploys an emotion recognition system in its stores. What must it do under the AI Act, and what does the GDPR add?
gold: Under AIA Art. 50(3) deployers of an emotion recognition system or a biometric categorisation system must inform the natural persons exposed to it of the operation of the system, and must process the personal data in accordance with the applicable data protection law. Because emotion recognition works on biometric data, GDPR Art. 9(1) is engaged: processing of biometric data for the purpose of uniquely identifying a natural person falls in the special categories whose processing is prohibited unless an Art. 9(2) exception applies. The AI Act information duty does not supply that legal basis.
